summary: Describes the IANA considerations for DNS parameters such as classes, resource record types, operation codes, and error codes. It is a Best Current Practice document and was later replaced.

plainLanguage.summary: IANA keeps the official list of DNS codes. This sets the rules for adding new ones to the list.

questions: how are new dns record types assigned
how many dns resource record types exist
subtitle: Rules for registering new DNS protocol codes

tldr.problem: DNS has many different parameter types (operation codes, response codes, resource record types and classes) that need to be assigned carefully to avoid conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines IANA assignment procedures for DNS parameters, specifying what procedure (IETF Standards Action, IETF Consensus, or Specification Required) applies to each parameter range.
tldr.outcome: It provides a centralized registry so new DNS extensions can be allocated without breaking existing implementations.

facts.label: Response code ranges
facts.value: 0-15 in header, extended to 12 bits via OPT record, up to 16 bits in TSIG/TKEY

facts.label: DNS classes
facts.value: Internet (1) dominates; Chaos (3) and Hesiod (4) for special uses

today: RFC 5395 obsoletes this document. The core idea of registering DNS parameters remains important, but RFC 5395 updates the specific assignment procedures and parameter space descriptions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is the system that translates domain names (like example.com) into IP addresses. It uses various codes and parameter values to function, including operation codes, error codes, resource record types, and address classes.

This RFC defines how IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) assigns new values in these different parameter spaces. Without these rules, people designing new DNS extensions might inadvertently use the same code numbers, causing conflicts when both extensions are deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a library where different people add new kinds of books. The librarian needs rules for how to tag new book types so everyone uses different tags.

sections.title: Query and Response Headers
sections.content:
A DNS query or response starts with a header containing several fields. The most important for parameter assignment are the OpCode (which specifies what kind of operation the query is performing), the RCODE (response code, indicating success or an error condition), and various flag bits.

Opcodes are currently assigned as follows: Query (0), IQuery (1), Status (2), Notify (4), and Update (5). Codes 3 and 6-15 are available. Response codes range from 0 (no error) to at least 21, with many more available. The RFC notes that response codes can appear in multiple locations (the header, OPT records, TSIG records, and TKEY records), and they all refer to the same code space except for code 16 which has different meanings in different contexts.
sections.plainLanguage: The header at the start of a DNS message tells what the message is for and how it went. The RFC sets rules for numbering new message types without breaking old DNS software.

sections.title: Resource Records: Types and Classes
sections.content:
All data stored in DNS is organized as Resource Records (RRs). Each RR has a TYPE (such as A for IPv4 address, MX for mail server) and a CLASS (such as IN for Internet). The RFC divides RR types into three categories: data types (which store actual data), query types (which can only appear in queries), and meta-types (which carry transient information).

Data types are typically numbered starting from 1, while query and meta-types use higher numbers. The RFC specifies different assignment procedures for different numeric ranges. For example, types 1-127 require IETF Consensus, while types 32768-65279 require only Specification Required (a less strict process). Classes work similarly, with Internet (IN, class 1) being the only globally used class, though classes like Chaos (3) and Hesiod (4) exist for specialized uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Records in DNS have a type (like 'where does the mail go') and a class (usually 'Internet'). The RFC decides how many types and classes can exist and who gets to create new ones.

sections.title: IANA Assignment Procedures
sections.content:
The RFC uses three main assignment procedures from RFC 2434. IETF Standards Action is the most restrictive: it requires publishing an Internet Standard. IETF Consensus requires discussion and rough agreement from the IETF community but not a full standards track publication. Specification Required is less formal, requiring only that an assignee provide a published specification of how the new parameter will be used.

For example, new opcodes require IETF Standards Action (most restrictive), new response codes require IETF Consensus (middle), and new resource record types in the middle numeric ranges require IETF Consensus (for widespread types) or Specification Required (for less common types). Some ranges are reserved for private use without any approval process. The intent is to protect core DNS functionality while allowing extension.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone wants to add a new DNS code, they need approval. Some codes need final approval from the whole IETF. Others just need a clear explanation. A few codes are free to use privately.

sections.title: Name Labeling and Security
sections.content:
DNS names are built from labels (like 'example' and 'com' in 'example.com'). The RFC notes that labels can use different formats: text labels (mostly ASCII) and binary labels. Labels are local to a DNS class, meaning the same name can have different meanings in different classes.

The RFC also mentions that the OPT resource record (type 41) is special: it extends various DNS field sizes, including the response code field from 4 bits to 12 bits. This allows for more response codes than the header alone could provide. The document defers to other RFCs for security considerations, noting that DNS security is covered separately in RFC 2535.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS names are built from pieces, and you can label them in different ways. One special type of record lets DNS systems talk about bigger numbers than usual.
